summary: Fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used for major depressive disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, bulimia nervosa, and panic disorder, and (with olanzapine) for depressive episodes of bipolar I disorder. It has notably long half-lives of the parent drug and active metabolite. It carries a boxed warning for increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults, and is contraindicated with MAOIs.
indications: Acute and maintenance treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD)
Acute and maintenance treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)
Acute and maintenance treatment of moderate-to-severe bulimia nervosa
Acute treatment of panic disorder, with or without agoraphobia
Acute treatment of depressive episodes associated with bipolar I disorder, in combination with olanzapine (not as monotherapy)

dosage.d: Initial 20 mg/day in the morning; max 80 mg/day
dosage.t: Increase after several weeks if needed; doses >20 mg/day once daily (am) or split am and noon
dosage.n: Full effect may be delayed 4 weeks or longer

dosage.t: If started at 10 mg/day, increase to 20 mg/day after 1 week; lower-weight children may stay at 10 mg/day
dosage.n: Approved from age 8 in MDD; not for children <7 years

dosage.d: Initial 20 mg/day; range 20-60 mg/day; max 80 mg/day
dosage.t: Increase after several weeks if needed; full effect may take 5 weeks or longer
dosage.n: Doses >20 mg may be once daily (am) or split am and noon

dosage.t: Increase to 20 mg/day after 2 weeks; further increases after several more weeks
dosage.n: Minimal experience above 20 mg in lower-weight children

dosage.t: May titrate up to 60 mg over several days
dosage.n: Only the 60 mg dose was superior to placebo; doses >60 mg/day not studied

dosage.d: Initial 10 mg/day; usual 20 mg/day; range 10-60 mg/day
dosage.t: Increase to 20 mg/day after 1 week; further increase after several weeks if needed

dosage.d: Fluoxetine 20 mg with olanzapine 5 mg once daily in evening; fluoxetine range 20-50 mg, olanzapine 5-12.5 mg
dosage.n: Safety above olanzapine 18 mg / fluoxetine 75 mg not evaluated in adults

dosage.d: Fluoxetine 20 mg with olanzapine 2.5 mg once daily in evening
dosage.n: Safety above olanzapine 12 mg / fluoxetine 50 mg not evaluated in pediatrics

admin: Administer orally, generally in the morning; may be taken with or without food.
Doses above 20 mg/day may be given once daily in the morning or divided between morning and noon.
In hepatic impairment, the elderly, or patients on multiple medications, use a lower or less frequent dose.
When combined with olanzapine, dose once daily in the evening without regard to meals.
Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting fluoxetine, and at least 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before starting an MAOI.
Taper rather than abruptly discontinue to limit discontinuation symptoms (note the long half-life).
moa: The exact mechanism is unknown but is presumed to result from inhibition of CNS neuronal reuptake of serotonin (5-HT), increasing serotonergic neurotransmission. Fluoxetine is a racemate; its active metabolite norfluoxetine is also a potent serotonin reuptake inhibitor.

absolute: Concomitant use with MAOIs intended to treat psychiatric disorders, or within 5 weeks of stopping fluoxetine, or within 14 days of stopping an MAOI (risk of serotonin syndrome)
Starting fluoxetine in a patient receiving linezolid or intravenous methylene blue
Concomitant use with pimozide (QT prolongation; CYP2D6 interaction)
Concomitant use with thioridazine, or within 5 weeks of discontinuing fluoxetine (QT prolongation)
relative: Conditions or drugs predisposing to QT prolongation
Volume depletion or risk of hyponatremia (elderly)
monitor: BOXED WARNING: Increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults (<24); monitor closely for clinical worsening and emergence of suicidality, especially early in therapy and after dose changes
Monitor for serotonin syndrome, especially with other serotonergic drugs
Screen for bipolar disorder before treating depression; monitor for activation of mania/hypomania
Monitor for abnormal bleeding when used with NSAIDs, aspirin, or warfarin
Monitor serum sodium for hyponatremia (especially elderly or volume-depleted)
Monitor for QT prolongation in at-risk patients

preg: Carefully weigh risks and benefits. Neonates exposed to SSRIs/SNRIs late in the third trimester have developed complications requiring prolonged hospitalization, respiratory support, and tube feeding. Untreated maternal depression also carries risk. Use the lowest effective dose and monitor the neonate after delivery.
lact: Fluoxetine and norfluoxetine pass into breast milk. Consider the long half-lives and potential for accumulation in the infant; weigh developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's clinical need and any potential effects, and monitor the infant for irritability, poor feeding, and somnolence.
renal: No routine dose adjustment is specified for renal impairment; because the active species are largely cleared by hepatic metabolism, standard dosing generally applies, but use general caution in significant impairment.
hepatic: Fluoxetine is extensively hepatically metabolized; clearance is reduced in hepatic impairment. Use a lower or less frequent dose in patients with hepatic impairment.

major: MAOIs (including linezolid, IV methylene blue): contraindicated - risk of serotonin syndrome
Pimozide: contraindicated - QT prolongation and increased pimozide levels
Thioridazine: contraindicated - QT prolongation and increased thioridazine levels
Other serotonergic drugs (triptans, tramadol, other SSRIs/SNRIs, lithium): serotonin syndrome risk
Drugs that prolong the QT interval (e.g., certain antipsychotics, Class IA/III antiarrhythmics, methadone)
moderate: CYP2D6 substrates (TCAs, antipsychotics, flecainide, propafenone): fluoxetine inhibits CYP2D6, raising their levels - reduce dose; effect persists weeks after stopping
Drugs affecting hemostasis (NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin): increased bleeding risk - monitor
Anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine): elevated levels and toxicity
Benzodiazepines (diazepam prolonged half-life; alprazolam increased levels/psychomotor decrement)
Lithium: increased or decreased levels and increased serotonergic effects - monitor
minor: Drugs tightly bound to plasma proteins (e.g., warfarin, digitoxin): possible shift in plasma concentrations
CYP3A4 substrates: clinically insignificant inhibition expected
interactions.food: Food does not affect systemic bioavailability (may delay absorption 1-2 hours, not clinically significant); may be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; additive CNS effects and worsened depression.
interactions.diagnostics: May prolong the QT interval on ECG; rare hyponatremia (check serum sodium) and abnormal bleeding parameters.

common: Nausea, diarrhea, anorexia/decreased appetite, dry mouth, dyspepsia
Yawning, flu syndrome, pharyngitis, sinusitis, vasodilatation
serious: BOXED WARNING: Increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias (including torsade de pointes)
rare: Allergic reactions / serious rash, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis
Pancytopenia, aplastic anemia, immune hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia
emergency: Suicidal thoughts or behavior, especially in patients <24 (boxed warning) - seek immediate help
Serotonin syndrome (agitation, hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability)
Syncope or palpitations suggesting arrhythmia/QT prolongation

monitoring: Suicidal ideation and clinical worsening, especially in patients <24 and after dose changes
Mood and emergence of mania/hypomania (screen for bipolar disorder first)
Signs of serotonin syndrome, particularly with other serotonergic agents
Serum sodium in elderly or volume-depleted patients
Bleeding when used with NSAIDs, aspirin, or anticoagulants
ECG/QT in at-risk patients or with QT-prolonging drugs
counsel: May be taken with or without food, usually in the morning to reduce insomnia.
Watch for and report any new or worsening depression, agitation, or thoughts of suicide, especially in young people.
Full benefit may take 4 weeks or longer; continue as prescribed.
Do not start or stop without telling your doctor; the drug stays in the body for weeks due to its long half-life.
Tell your doctor about all medicines - especially MAOIs, other antidepressants, triptans, tramadol, NSAIDs/aspirin/warfarin, and pimozide or thioridazine.
Report muscle rigidity, fever, fast heartbeat, confusion, or shivering (possible serotonin syndrome).
Do not become pregnant without discussing risks; inform your doctor if pregnant or breastfeeding.
pk: Long; active drug persists weeks after stopping
pearls: BOXED WARNING: Antidepressants increase the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults (<24); monitor closely, especially early and after dose changes.
Contraindicated with MAOIs - allow 14 days after stopping an MAOI before starting, and at least 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before an MAOI (long half-life).
Very long half-lives of fluoxetine and active metabolite norfluoxetine mean self-tapering and persistent drug interactions for weeks after discontinuation.
Potent CYP2D6 inhibitor - raises levels of TCAs, many antipsychotics, and certain antiarrhythmics; reduce risperidone to <=8 mg/day when combined.
Contraindicated with pimozide and thioridazine due to QT prolongation.
Screen for bipolar disorder before treating depression to avoid precipitating mania.
Bulimia nervosa requires the higher 60 mg/day dose for efficacy.
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the normal schedule. Do not double up. Because fluoxetine has a very long half-life, a single missed dose is unlikely to cause withdrawal symptoms.
overdose: The most common features are seizures, somnolence, nausea, tachycardia, and vomiting; serious effects can include coma, delirium, ECG abnormalities (QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmias including torsade de pointes), hypotension, mania, NMS-like reactions, and syncope. There is no specific antidote. Provide supportive care - ensure airway, oxygenation, and ventilation; monitor cardiac rhythm and vital signs; give activated charcoal; do not induce emesis. Forced diuresis, dialysis, and hemoperfusion are unlikely to help given the large volume of distribution. Consider multi-drug ingestion (especially TCAs). Contact a poison control center (1-800-222-1222).
